title: Care for creation
hookLine: a saint sings to Brother Sun and Sister Water, and a pope borrows his first words

cards: Brother Sun. Sister Moon. Brother Wind.

Sister Water. In his Canticle of the Creatures, Francis of Assisi praises God for each of them by name, as if he were introducing his relatives. Then he calls the earth itself our sister and mother, who feeds us.
Stanza after stanza, the canticle repeats the same words in the old Italian of his day: laudato si', praise be to you.
When Pope Francis wrote a letter about the environment, he took its name from that refrain, and its subtitle reads: on care for our common home. Today, care for creation.

teach.h: VERY GOOD, BECAUSE GOD MADE IT.
teach.b: First, the goodness. Genesis looks back over everything made, and says, in the Douay-Rheims: "And God saw all the things that he had made, and they were very good."
Very good, and the verse gives no reason but that God made them. In Catholic teaching, creation has worth because God made it, not only because people need it. Second, who owns it.
A psalm says, in the Douay-Rheims: "The earth is the Lord's and the fulness thereof." People are tenants, not landlords. The Catechism says the dominion Genesis gives humanity isn't absolute.
It's a trust, and it has to respect the integrity of creation.

teach.h: THE CRY OF THE EARTH AND THE POOR.
teach.b: Third, the earth and the poor together. Pope Francis wrote that damage to the environment falls hardest on the most vulnerable, and asked his readers to hear both the cry of the earth and the cry of the poor.
A poisoned river is an injustice to whoever lives downstream.
So care for creation isn't a separate cause beside the rest of this block; it's dignity, the poor and solidarity, all at once, with soil and water in the picture. Fourth, time.

teach.h: A HOME FOR THOSE NOT YET BORN.
teach.b: Our common home is shared across the years, not only across the globe. The Catechism names the generations to come, and Pope Francis wrote that the world people have received belongs also to those who will follow them.
Somebody not yet born will drink from the same river.

how: Catholics read Pope Francis's Laudato Si' in parishes and schools, some keep a Season of Creation in the fall, and Francis of Assisi's canticle is prayed and sung around his feast day.

o: protecting nature by keeping people out of it entirely
tending the earth as God's, for the poor and the future
a yearly blessing of pets, gardens and farm animals

games.q: care for creation — tap the pairs.
p: God's verdict on all he made

s: in Genesis, creation is called very good because people can use it
the verse says only that God saw all he had made, and it was very good.
Pope Francis's letter on the environment takes its name from Francis of Assisi's canticle
laudato si': praise be to you, the canticle's refrain.
the Catechism treats human dominion over creation as unlimited
it says dominion isn't absolute; it must respect the integrity of creation.

games.q: you're Francis of Assisi, singing praise to God for the things he made. what do you call the sun?
games.why: brother sun, sister moon, and the earth our sister and mother. Francis sings to creation as family, not as property.

practice: Sister Water, Francis called it: let the water you'll use today come to mind, the shower, the sink, the kettle, the dishes, the glass by your bed, and pick one place to use less, and exactly how: a shorter shower, the tap off while you brush, a full load instead of half.
Then follow that water downstream in your mind, to the people and creatures who share it, now and later. If you pray, you can give thanks for it.

wordCard.voice: Care for creation. In Catholic teaching, the earth is the Lord's, very good in itself, and held in trust for the poor and for generations to come. Today's word.

orig.note: Hebrew: very good. God's verdict on all he made, in Genesis.

carryVoice: Your line: our common home. Somebody downstream, and somebody not yet born, shares every river. Go gently.
